title: The Teleporter Paradox & Personal Identity
rootClaim: Destructive teleportation (dematerializing a body and scanning it to assemble an exact replica on Mars) kills the original person and creates a duplicate.

branches.text: Numerical identity requires continuity of physical matter or unbroken spatiotemporal paths, which teleportation severs.

children.text: The Double-Teleportation Case: If the scanner fails to destroy the Earth body while creating the Mars replica, two conscious beings exist simultaneously, proving identity is not preserved.
Parfit's Relation R: Identity is not what matters in survival; psychological connectedness and continuity are what matter, even if branching occurs.
Ego-Death Reality: From the first-person perspective, your stream of consciousness permanently ends on Earth when the dematerializer fires.
Physical Criterion: Personal identity is grounded in the continuous persistence of the living organism and its specific physical neural tissue.
Gradual Atomic Replacement: Biological cells naturally replace all their constituent atoms over years without destroying identity, making specific physical matter irrelevant.
Spatiotemporal Continuity: Natural cellular replacement maintains a continuous physical trajectory through time, whereas teleportation creates a spatial gap.

branches.text: Psychological Continuity Criterion: Personal identity consists in the preservation of psychological patterns, memories, character traits, and mental states.

children.text: The Mars duplicate possesses perfect memory recall, identical beliefs, feelings, and character structure, making them functionally the same individual.
Duplication Fallacy: Two distinct physical objects cannot be numerically identical to one another (Leibniz's Law of Identity).
Information Realism: The self is a high-level informational pattern; medium of storage and physical instance transitions are irrelevant to pattern identity.
Subjective Illusion: Conflating qualitative similarity (looking and acting identical) with numerical identity (being one and the same entity).

definitions.description: The relation an object bears only to itself (being one and the same entity over time).
The relation between two distinct entities that share all intrinsic properties and features.
The overlap of chains of memory, belief, preference, and character traits connecting a person at different times.
Derek Parfit's concept of psychological connectedness and continuity with any cause, which he argues is what really matters in survival.
